## `docs/briefing/src/parts/11-part1-b.html`

```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-2">2&nbsp;&nbsp;What a unicorn actually requires</h2>

<p class="lede">
  You asked for a path to a billion-dollar company. The useful response is not encouragement; it is
  arithmetic. The arithmetic has one clear conclusion, and it should change what you build next.
</p>

<div class="callout warn">
  <span class="label">Said once, plainly</span>
  <p>
    Nobody can promise you a unicorn, and any adviser who does is selling something. Outcomes at
    that scale are rare enough that no plan produces one on demand. What a plan <em>can</em> do is
    make the outcome possible instead of arithmetically impossible &mdash; and most companies
    foreclose it early, by choosing a price. That is the whole content of this section.
  </p>
</div>

<h3>Working backwards from the number</h3>

<p>
  A $1&nbsp;billion valuation is a multiple applied to revenue. Software businesses have traded
  across a wide band depending on growth, margin and the market's mood, and I am not going to invent
  a current figure. Take <strong>10&times; forward revenue</strong> as a working assumption and
  treat the answer as an order of magnitude, not a target. <span class="ev a">ASSUMPTION</span>
</p>

<div class="arith">
  <div class="r"><span>Target valuation</span><span>$1,000,000,000</span></div>
  <div class="r"><span>Working revenue multiple</span><span>&divide; 10</span></div>
  <div class="r tot"><span>Annual recurring revenue required</span><span>$100,000,000</span></div>
</div>

<p>
  So: <strong>roughly $100M of annual recurring revenue.</strong> Everything now turns on one
  variable &mdash; what one archive pays you per year.
</p>

<h3>Four ways to get to $100M, and what each demands</h3>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 8%"></th>
      <th style="width: 26%">Model</th>
      <th style="width: 18%">Revenue per archive/yr</th>
      <th style="width: 18%">Paying archives needed</th>
      <th>What has to be true</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>A</strong></td>
      <td>Mass-market consumer subscription</td>
      <td class="t-num">$120</td>
      <td class="t-num"><strong>833,000</strong></td>
      <td>
        A consumer product with viral or near-zero-cost acquisition. You do not have one, and §3
        explains why this category structurally resists it.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>B</strong></td>
      <td>Premium consumer subscription</td>
      <td class="t-num">$600</td>
      <td class="t-num"><strong>167,000</strong></td>
      <td>
        Still a very large number of families paying meaningfully every year, sustained for years.
        Possible; hard.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>C</strong></td>
      <td>Concierge: guided capture plus preservation</td>
      <td class="t-num">$2,000</td>
      <td class="t-num"><strong>50,000</strong></td>
      <td>
        Reachable through channels rather than advertising.
        <strong>The most plausible consumer-facing route.</strong> Margin risk &mdash; see below.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>D</strong></td>
      <td>Institutional accounts</td>
      <td class="t-num">$20,000</td>
      <td class="t-num"><strong>5,000</strong></td>
      <td>
        Sold to organisations that already hold the relationship and the occasion. 5,000 accounts is
        a normal B2B outcome, not a fantasy.
      </td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<div class="callout ok">
  <span class="label">The conclusion, which is the whole point of the section</span>
  <p>
    <strong>A low-priced consumer subscription cannot reach this outcome for this product.</strong>
    833,000 families paying every year, in a category where people demonstrably postpone the thing
    for decades, is not a plan &mdash; it is a wish. Price high, sell through institutions, or both.
    Everything in Part III follows from this line. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
  </p>
</div>

<h3>The margin trap inside model C</h3>

<p>
  Model C reaches high revenue per archive by putting a person in the loop: someone conducts the
  interview well, someone helps an eighty-year-old through the review queue. That works, and it is
  probably how you should start. But a business whose costs scale with headcount earns a services
  multiple, not a software multiple &mdash; and at a services multiple, $100M of revenue is not a
  billion-dollar company.
</p>

<div class="flow">
  concierge-led product-led ───────────── ─────────── high revenue per archive high revenue per
  archive costs scale with people ──▶ costs scale with software gross margin ~40–60% gross margin
  ~75–85% services multiple software multiple │ ▲ └──── use it to LEARN, then productise ──┘ the
  repeatable parts
</div>

<p>
  The resolution is sequencing, not choosing. Run concierge deliberately and temporarily: it is the
  fastest way to learn what a good interview actually is, and every hour a human spends is a
  specification for something to automate. Then move each repeatable piece into the product and
  watch gross margin climb. If gross margin is not rising by the fiftieth archive, the concierge
  model has become the company. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
</p>

<div class="page-break"></div>
<h3>The unit economics worksheet</h3>

<p>
  You cannot price until you know what one archive costs to serve, and you do not know yet, because
  the providers that cost money have never been connected. Fill this in during Horizon&nbsp;1
  &mdash; it is a two-day task and it determines every number in Part III.
</p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 44%">Cost line</th>
      <th style="width: 20%">Driver</th>
      <th>Status</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td colspan="3" class="eyebrow" style="margin: 0">One-time, per archive</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Speech-to-text on real recordings</td>
      <td>hours &times; per-hour rate</td>
      <td><span class="ev u">UNKNOWN</span> no provider connected</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Document OCR</td>
      <td>pages</td>
      <td><span class="ev u">UNKNOWN</span></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Interview facilitation, if concierge</td>
      <td>hours &times; loaded cost</td>
      <td><span class="ev u">UNKNOWN</span></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Onboarding and review hand-holding</td>
      <td>hours</td>
      <td><span class="ev u">UNKNOWN</span> &mdash; expect this to be the surprise</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td colspan="3" class="eyebrow" style="margin: 0">
        Every year, per archive, <em>forever</em>
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Object storage for originals</td>
      <td>GB &times; rate &times; 12</td>
      <td><span class="ev u">UNKNOWN</span></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Backups and a second region</td>
      <td>storage &times; copies</td>
      <td><span class="ev u">UNKNOWN</span></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Retrieval, embedding and composition</td>
      <td>queries</td>
      <td>small; local adapters are cheap</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Support, including emotionally heavy support</td>
      <td>tickets &times; minutes</td>
      <td><span class="ev u">UNKNOWN</span></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<div class="callout danger">
  <span class="label">The line that can quietly bankrupt this company</span>
  <p>
    <strong>Storage is perpetual; subscriptions are not.</strong> You are promising to preserve
    something. If a family pays for three years and stops, and you keep the archive because deleting
    a dead parent's recordings feels monstrous, you have taken on an unfunded liability that grows
    with every customer you win. Video makes it far worse than audio &mdash; the same hour of
    material can be one to two orders of magnitude larger.
  </p>
  <p>
    Two structural answers, and you should take both: <strong>(1) default to audio</strong>, price
    video as a deliberate upgrade; <strong>(2) fund preservation explicitly</strong> &mdash; either
    the subscription must continue for the archive to be hosted (and export is always free, so
    nothing is held hostage), or a one-time <em>preservation payment</em> is priced to cover storage
    for a stated term. Whichever you choose, say it in plain words on the pricing page before anyone
    pays. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
  </p>
</div>

<p>
  A perpetual-care endowment is the model cemeteries use, and it may carry trust, escrow or reserve
  obligations depending on jurisdiction. Put it on the list for counsel in §5 rather than designing
  it yourself. <span class="ev u">UNKNOWN &mdash; legal question</span>
</p>

<h3>What I would actually aim at</h3>
<p>
  Not $100M. Aim at the milestone that makes the next one possible, and let the arithmetic above
  tell you only one thing: <strong>do not choose a cheap price.</strong> A cheap price is the single
  decision that forecloses the outcome you asked me about, and it is usually made casually, in an
  afternoon, by a founder who feels awkward asking for money.
</p>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/12-part1-c.html`

```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-3">3&nbsp;&nbsp;The five structural problems</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Not risks &mdash; risks are in §18. These are properties of the category that will not go away no
  matter how well you execute. Each one has an answer. None of the answers is &ldquo;work
  harder&rdquo;.
</p>

<h3>Problem 1 &mdash; The refusal does not demo</h3>
<p>
  A voice clone sells itself in fifteen seconds. Your most important behaviour is
  <em>declining to answer</em>, which is invisible in a screenshot and reads as a limitation to
  anyone who has not thought about it for ten minutes. You are selling the absence of a failure, and
  absences do not demo. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">What to do about it</p>
<ul>
  <li>
    <strong>Demo the pair, never the answer alone.</strong> Ask a question the archive can answer,
    then ask one it cannot, in the same breath. The second screen is the product. Your existing
    Figures 8 and 9 already do this &mdash; make it the fixed shape of every demo you ever give.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Demo to the storyteller, not the buyer.</strong> The parent is the one for whom the
    refusal is worth money. Watch an older person realise that the system will not put words in
    their mouth; that reaction is your marketing asset, and you cannot script it.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Show the click-through.</strong> Answer &rarr; cited sentence &rarr; transcript &rarr;
    the actual recording, in one continuous motion. That chain is a foreign-key walk, not a citation
    string, and it is the thing competitors cannot fake.
  </li>
</ul>

<h3>Problem 2 &mdash; The buyer is not the user</h3>
<p>
  An adult child finds you, is moved, and pays. Then the entire value of the purchase depends on a
  seventy-eight-year-old who has never seen your website agreeing to spend hours recording, and then
  reviewing what was recorded. Your product correctly refuses to proceed without them &mdash; which
  is right, and which means
  <strong>your conversion rate is decided by a person you cannot market to.</strong>
  <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">What to do about it</p>
<ul>
  <li>
    <strong>Build the asking artifact.</strong> The hardest moment in this product is a child asking
    a parent. Give them the words: a letter, a card, a page written to be forwarded, that explains
    what this is and &mdash; crucially &mdash; what it refuses to do. This is a product feature, not
    a marketing asset, and it does not exist yet.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Make the first session absurdly easy.</strong> No account for the parent on day one if
    you can avoid it. A phone call, a scheduled session, someone else driving.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Measure the funnel that matters:</strong> payment &rarr; storyteller consents &rarr;
    first recording &rarr; <strong>first approved memory</strong>. That last step is your real
    activation event. Everything before it is a promise.
  </li>
</ul>

<h3>Problem 3 &mdash; There is no occasion</h3>
<p>
  Everyone intends to do this and almost nobody does, which is the observation the product is
  founded on. The uncomfortable corollary:
  <strong>the same force that creates the market suppresses the purchase.</strong> Intent without a
  trigger produces a bookmarked website and no revenue. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">What to do about it</p>
<p>
  Stop trying to manufacture urgency &mdash; you cannot, and attempting it lands you squarely in the
  guilt mechanics the product refuses. Instead,
  <strong>attach to occasions other people already own</strong>:
</p>
<div class="two-col">
  <div>
    <ul>
      <li>A milestone birthday &mdash; seventieth, eightieth</li>
      <li>Retirement</li>
      <li>A diagnosis, or a hospice admission</li>
      <li>Moving out of a long-held home</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
  <div>
    <ul>
      <li>A first grandchild</li>
      <li>A significant anniversary</li>
      <li>Estate or will preparation</li>
      <li>Citizenship, or a return visit to a country left behind</li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</div>
<p>
  Every one of those moments is already attended by somebody &mdash; a wealth adviser, a hospice
  social worker, a senior-living director, a family lawyer.
  <strong
    >That is the argument for §10, and it is the single most important strategic idea in this
    document after the pricing conclusion in §2.</strong
  >
</p>

<div class="page-break"></div>
<h3>Problem 4 &mdash; You have deliberately removed your retention levers</h3>
<p>
  The standard subscription playbook retains customers by bringing them back: digests, reminders,
  streaks, nudges. Your product has <strong>no notification scheduler at all</strong>, on purpose,
  because reminders about a parent's mortality become guilt with almost no effort.
  <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span>
</p>

<p>
  That is the correct decision and I would not reverse it. But be clear about what it costs: an
  archive that is finished is an archive nobody opens, and a subscription nobody opens is a
  subscription somebody eventually cancels.
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">What to do about it</p>
<ul>
  <li>
    <strong>Sell custody, not engagement.</strong> Nobody expects to visit their safe-deposit box
    monthly. Price and describe this as preservation. Then
    <em>do not measure daily actives</em> &mdash; you will panic at a number that means nothing
    here.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Let the family be the retention.</strong> Each additional family member with access is
    another person for whom cancelling is unthinkable. Members-per-archive is a retention metric;
    sessions-per-week is not.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Growth, not nudges.</strong> An archive can gain new chapters years later. Offer that
    when the family initiates, and only then &mdash; a returning customer is welcome, a chased one
    is a violation of the thing you built.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Handle the true test honestly:</strong> the renewal that arrives after the storyteller
    has died. Decide the policy now, in §17, while it is abstract. You will not think clearly about
    it the first time it happens to a real family.
  </li>
</ul>

<h3>Problem 5 &mdash; The verdict arrives years late</h3>
<p>
  A family cannot tell whether the archive is any good until they need it &mdash; which may be a
  decade away, and often after the person has died. This breaks two loops at once:
  <strong>word of mouth is slow</strong>, because nobody has the experience that makes them
  evangelise; and <strong>your quality feedback is slow</strong>, because the failure mode &mdash; a
  thin archive, the wrong questions asked, the important story never told &mdash; only becomes
  visible when it is far too late to fix. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">What to do about it</p>
<ul>
  <li>
    <strong>Manufacture an early verdict.</strong> Deliver something the family holds within weeks:
    the printed biography draft, a short edited audio piece, a set of stories read at a birthday. An
    artefact that lands while everyone is alive is what converts a customer into an advocate a
    decade early.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Grade the archive, not the software.</strong> Build a coverage view &mdash; which
    decades, which relationships, which themes are thin. That turns an unmeasurable outcome into a
    visible gap the family can close now.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Interview quality is the actual product.</strong> Two archives with identical software
    differ enormously based on what was asked. Treat the question set as your core IP, version it,
    and improve it deliberately. This is also what the concierge phase in §2 is for.
  </li>
</ul>

<div class="callout">
  <span class="label">Read these five together</span>
  <p>
    They all point the same direction:
    <strong>do not run this as a self-serve consumer subscription.</strong> Sell high-value archives
    through people who own the occasion, deliver something tangible early, and let custody &mdash;
    not engagement &mdash; carry retention. Parts II and III are that plan.
  </p>
</div>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/13-part1-d.html`

```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-4">4&nbsp;&nbsp;The three assets you actually have</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Section 3 was the honest accounting of what is hard. This is the honest accounting of what is rare
  &mdash; and all three of these are more valuable than the traction you do not yet have.
</p>

<h3>Asset 1 &mdash; The refusal is a position, and the market is moving toward it</h3>

<p>
  You are not a slightly-safer version of the simulation products. You are the opposite category,
  and you can say so in one sentence that a stranger understands:
  <em
    >we record what a living person actually said, we show you where every sentence came from, and
    we will never pretend to be them.</em
  >
</p>

<p>This is worth more than it looks, for three reasons:</p>
<ul>
  <li>
    <strong>Every bad story about a griefbot is your advertisement.</strong> You do not need to
    attack anyone. You need to be the obvious thing a journalist calls for the contrasting quote,
    and the obvious thing a reader searches for afterwards.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>It is the only version institutions can touch.</strong> A hospice, a university archive,
    a bank's private-client arm, a religious community &mdash; none of them can put their name on a
    product that simulates the dead. The refusal is not a constraint on your enterprise sales; it is
    the precondition for having any. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>It is enforced, not promised.</strong> Anyone can claim restraint. You can point at a
    policy compiler that refuses the document, a function that discards a first-person answer, and a
    test that fails if someone removes either. That is a difference you can demonstrate in a
    meeting.
  </li>
</ul>

<div class="callout warn">
  <span class="label">The cost of this position</span>
  <p>
    You will spend the rest of the company's life being mistaken for the thing you refuse to be.
    Budget for it: a permanent, prominent, plainly-worded explanation, repeated more often than
    feels necessary, forever. The <em>Trust and consent</em> page already does this well &mdash;
    treat it as a primary surface, not a footer link.
  </p>
</div>

<h3>Asset 2 &mdash; The machinery underneath might be the larger company</h3>

<p>
  Strip away the family archive and look at what you built: a consent document that compiles to an
  enforceable policy; a pure authorisation function whose obligations become part of the SQL query
  rather than a filter applied afterwards; retrieval that cannot see what the viewer may not know
  exists; a verification step that drops any sentence its citation does not support; forced tenant
  isolation at the database; and deletion that is resumable and produces a receipt.
</p>

<p>
  That is a general answer to a question a great many organisations are being asked right now:
  <em
    >how do you let an AI system read sensitive material without it leaking, inventing, or exceeding
    what the subject agreed to?</em
  >
  Adjacent buyers exist in oral history and archives, hospice and palliative care, estate and
  private-client services, journalism and documentary research, and any regulated setting where an
  answer must cite and abstain.
  <span class="ev u"
    >UNKNOWN &mdash; none of this is validated; it is a hypothesis with a strong prior</span
  >
</p>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision &mdash; do not make this one yet</span>
  <p>
    The temptation, in about month four, will be to pivot from families to infrastructure because
    enterprise revenue looks closer. Resist it until you have run §8. Two reasons: the consumer
    product is where you learn what the consent model must actually do, and an infrastructure
    company with no application is a crowded, undifferentiated place to arrive.
  </p>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>Recommendation:</strong> treat this as an option you hold, not a plan you execute. Keep
    the packages cleanly separated (they already are), take an enterprise conversation if one walks
    in, and revisit deliberately at the §16 branch point &mdash; not in a discouraged week.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="page-break"></div>
<h3>Asset 3 &mdash; Verifiable honesty, in a market with almost none of it</h3>

<p>
  You have a document that says <em>&ldquo;Not ready for a real family's memories&rdquo;</em>, a
  table listing eight integrations that were written and never executed, and a product that answers
  a question it cannot support with a fixed sentence declining to answer. Nobody does this. It is
  worth a great deal, in three specific ways.
</p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 24%">With</th>
      <th>Why it converts</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Storytellers</strong></td>
      <td>
        They are deciding whether to hand you the most private material they have. Restraint they
        can verify is the only argument that works on someone genuinely reluctant &mdash; and the
        reluctant ones are the ones with the stories worth keeping.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Institutions</strong></td>
      <td>
        Procurement, ethics committees and compliance teams are trying to find out what you are
        hiding. Handing over the readiness document unprompted collapses months of that.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Investors</strong></td>
      <td>
        You have no traction. What you have instead is evidence about the founder: a complete,
        tested, documented product with the hard parts finished and the gaps named. For a
        pre-traction round, that <em>is</em> the diligence. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
      </td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<div class="callout ok">
  <span class="label">A move I would make in month one</span>
  <p>
    <strong>Publish the production-readiness document.</strong> Publicly, on the site, including the
    verdict and the list of things that were never run. Almost nobody will do this, which is exactly
    why it works: it makes every other claim you make credible, and it costs you nothing you were
    going to get away with anyway. If it later becomes commercially awkward, that is a signal you
    have started overstating &mdash; which is the failure mode this company most needs an alarm for.
  </p>
</div>

<h3>And what you do not have</h3>
<p>For completeness, because the assets above are easy to over-read:</p>
<div class="kv">
  <div><span>A customer</span><span>none</span></div>
  <div><span>A price</span><span>not set</span></div>
  <div><span>A deployed system</span><span>none &mdash; no production auth exists</span></div>
  <div><span>Legal clearance on any consent wording</span><span>none</span></div>
  <div><span>A distribution channel</span><span>none</span></div>
  <div>
    <span>Cleared rights to the name</span><span>codename, pending trademark clearance</span>
  </div>
  <div><span>Evidence anyone will pay</span><span>none</span></div>
</div>

<p style="margin-top: 4mm">
  Every one of those is addressed in Part II or III, in the order that a rational person would
  address them. The order is not the order they feel urgent in.
</p>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/20-part2-a.html`

```html
<div class="part-divider">
  <div class="kicker">Part II</div>
  <h2>Getting online safely</h2>
  <p>
    The next eight weeks, in the order they must actually happen. This is the part to act on this
    week.
  </p>
</div>

<h2 id="sec-5">5&nbsp;&nbsp;Horizon 0: the decisions only you can make</h2>

<div class="horizon">
  <span class="h-n">Horizon 0</span>
  <span>Nothing here is engineering. All of it blocks engineering.</span>
  <span class="h-when">Weeks 0&ndash;2</span>
</div>

<p class="lede">
  Seven decisions. Two of them have hard deadlines imposed by outside parties and should start on
  day one because they take weeks of somebody else's time.
</p>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision 1 &mdash; The name</span>
  <p>
    Your own README says EverEcho is
    <em>&ldquo;a working codename pending trademark clearance&rdquo;</em>.
    <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span> You cannot build a brand, buy a domain properly, print
    anything, or sign a channel partner on a name you may have to abandon. Every week you delay
    makes the eventual rename more expensive.
  </p>
  <p>
    You did one thing very well here: the product name lives in configuration
    (<code>PRODUCT_NAME</code>), so renaming the software is a settings change, not a refactor. The
    expensive part is everything outside the repository.
  </p>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>Recommendation:</strong> start clearance <strong>on day one</strong>, in every
    jurisdiction you intend to operate in, in the relevant classes. If it is not clearly clearable
    within three weeks, <strong>rename now</strong> rather than hope. Budget this as the first
    professional-services money you spend.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision 2 &mdash; Where the company and the data live</span>
  <p>
    Configuration currently says <code>JURISDICTION=IN</code> and <code>DATA_REGION=local</code>.
    <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span> Those were sensible development defaults and they are now a
    strategic choice with legal consequences: which law governs consent, where the database
    physically sits, whether using a US-hosted AI provider constitutes a cross-border transfer, and
    which regulator you answer to.
  </p>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>Recommendation:</strong> incorporate and host where your first ten families are, not
    where you imagine your hundred-thousandth will be. Keep the region a configuration value, as it
    already is, and treat a second region as a Horizon&nbsp;3 problem. Do not architect for a
    geography you have no customers in.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision 3 &mdash; Engage counsel, with a written brief</span>
  <p>
    This is the highest-leverage thing you will do in the next month, it is blocking item&nbsp;1 on
    your own readiness list, and it runs on somebody else's calendar. Start it in week one. The
    brief is on the next page &mdash; do not send &ldquo;please review our privacy policy&rdquo;,
    send the questions.
  </p>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>Recommendation:</strong> find counsel with data-protection experience specifically, not
    a general commercial lawyer. Ask them directly whether they have advised on special-category
    data and on what happens to personal data when the subject dies. If they hesitate on the second
    question, keep looking.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision 4 &mdash; Name the accountable person</span>
  <p>
    Blocking item&nbsp;8:
    <em>the incident runbook says &ldquo;escalate&rdquo; and there is no one to escalate to.</em>
    <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span> If you are solo, the answer is you &mdash; but it must be
    written down, with a name, in the runbook, on the support page, and in whatever you sign with a
    customer. An accountability that is implied is an accountability that evaporates at exactly the
    wrong moment.
  </p>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>Recommendation:</strong> name yourself today, in writing, in
    <code>INCIDENT_RUNBOOK.md</code>, and commit it. Replace the name when you hire someone; never
    let the field be empty.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision 5 &mdash; Audio-first, or audio and video</span>
  <p>
    From the storage arithmetic in §2: video can be one to two orders of magnitude larger than audio
    for the same hour, and you are promising preservation. This decision sets your cost base
    permanently and is very painful to reverse once families have uploaded video.
  </p>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>Recommendation:</strong> <strong>audio by default</strong>, video as an explicitly
    priced upgrade with its own storage term stated. Photographs and documents are cheap; treat them
    as included and encourage them, since they carry enormous emotional weight per megabyte.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision 6 &mdash; Provisional price</span>
  <p>
    Your pricing page currently sets no price at all. <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span> You cannot
    run §8 without one, and §2 established the one thing you must not do: choose a cheap one.
  </p>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>Recommendation:</strong> pick a provisional number in week two using §9, and hold it for
    the first ten families. Do not discount to close &mdash; a discounted first cohort teaches you
    nothing about willingness to pay, which is the only thing that cohort exists to teach you.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision 7 &mdash; A stance, not a commitment, on money</span>
  <p>
    Bootstrap or raise changes your hiring, your speed and how much of §6 you do yourself. §14
    argues it properly. You need a provisional stance now because it determines whether you spend
    the next eight weeks building or talking.
  </p>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>Recommendation:</strong> assume bootstrap through §8. Ten paying families is the
    cheapest, fastest, most honest fundraising asset you can build, and it is worth more in a pitch
    than any deck you could write instead.
  </p>
</div>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/21-part2-b.html`

```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h3>The brief for counsel</h3>

<p>
  Send these as questions. A lawyer given a document to review returns comments; a lawyer given
  questions returns answers you can act on. Nothing below is legal advice &mdash; it is the list of
  things I would not launch without an answer to.
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">Consent itself</p>
<ol class="runbook">
  <li>
    <strong>Does our consent flow constitute valid, informed consent</strong> in each jurisdiction
    we will operate in? We record a versioned, hashed policy document plus a
    &ldquo;teach-back&rdquo; in which the storyteller restates in their own words what they agreed
    to. <em>Does the teach-back help, hurt, or do nothing legally?</em>
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Special-category data.</strong> The product explicitly recognises health, financial,
    religious, political, sexual-orientation and biometric categories, because life stories contain
    them. What lawful basis applies, and what additional safeguards are required?
    <span class="ev v">VERIFIED &mdash; these are enum values in the schema</span>
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Withdrawal.</strong> Consent can be narrowed or revoked at any time and takes effect on
    the next authorisation check, including on queued background work. Does our implementation
    satisfy the withdrawal right, and what must we do about material already derived?
  </li>
</ol>

<p class="eyebrow">The people who never agreed</p>
<ol class="runbook">
  <li>
    <strong>Third parties inside memories.</strong> A story about a living brother contains that
    brother's personal data, and he has not consented to anything.
    <em>What are our obligations to people who appear in someone else's memories?</em> This is the
    legal question I would ask first, because it has no obvious technical answer and it is present
    in essentially every archive.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Minors appearing in memories.</strong> We refuse to create profiles for minors, but a
    grandmother's story mentions her grandchildren by name. What follows from that?
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Contributors.</strong> A contributor may propose corrections and context about the
    storyteller. What have they consented to, and what have they asserted about others?
  </li>
</ol>

<p class="eyebrow">Death, which this product cannot avoid</p>
<ol class="runbook">
  <li>
    <strong>Whose rights are they after death?</strong> Data-protection rights in a deceased person
    are treated differently across jurisdictions and we must not guess. Who may then exercise
    access, correction, export and deletion &mdash; and who may <em>refuse</em> those on the
    deceased's behalf?
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Is our succession directive legally effective?</strong> A storyteller names a steward
    with narrowly delegated tasks. How does that interact with a will, with probate, and with an
    executor who disagrees? What happens if the steward and the family conflict?
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Standing instructions.</strong> If a storyteller says &ldquo;never show this to my
    son&rdquo;, is that enforceable after death, and against whom?
  </li>
</ol>

<p class="eyebrow">Commercial and structural</p>
<ol class="runbook">
  <li>
    <strong>Cross-border processing.</strong> If we enable a hosted speech-to-text or composition
    provider in another country, what is required? We can contractually forbid provider training and
    set zero retention &mdash; is that sufficient?
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>The preservation model.</strong> If we take a one-time payment in exchange for storing
    something for a long or indefinite term, does that create trust, escrow or reserve obligations?
    (See §9.)
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>The refundable deposit.</strong> We take a deposit refundable at any time, for any
    reason, with no conversation required. Confirm the terms, the accounting treatment, and any
    consumer-protection requirements.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Binding the prohibitions.</strong> We want the refusal of voice cloning, likeness
    generation, persona chat and posthumous simulation to survive a change of management or an
    acquisition. What is the strongest available instrument &mdash; constitutional documents, a
    golden share, contractual covenants to customers, or something else? (This is §17 and it matters
    more than it sounds.)
  </li>
</ol>

<div class="callout warn">
  <span class="label">Expect one of these answers to be expensive</span>
  <p>
    My prediction, offered as a prediction and not a fact:
    <strong
      >question 4 &mdash; third parties inside memories &mdash; will come back harder than you
      expect</strong
    >, and may require a product change such as a redaction path, a named-person objection route, or
    narrower default sharing. Better to learn that in week three than in year two.
    <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
  </p>
</div>

<h3>What Horizon 0 produces</h3>
<ul class="check">
  <li>A name you own, or a decision to rename made deliberately</li>
  <li>An incorporated entity and a chosen data region</li>
  <li>Counsel engaged, brief sent, first answers scheduled</li>
  <li>A named accountable person, committed to the repository</li>
  <li>Audio-first decided; video priced separately or deferred</li>
  <li>A provisional price you will not discount</li>
  <li>A provisional stance on funding</li>
  <li>The pricing-page tense corrected, so the site claims nothing untrue</li>
</ul>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/22-part2-c.html`

```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-6">
  6&nbsp;&nbsp;Horizon 1: from &ldquo;runs on a laptop&rdquo; to &ldquo;safe to launch&rdquo;
</h2>

<div class="horizon">
  <span class="h-n">Horizon 1</span>
  <span>Engineering and operations. Synthetic data only, throughout.</span>
  <span class="h-when">Weeks 2&ndash;8</span>
</div>

<h3>First, the three clocks</h3>

<p>
  The most common way a founder loses a month is by treating every task as though it runs on their
  own clock. It does not. Sort the work by whose calendar it depends on, and start everything on
  somebody else's calendar <strong>in week one</strong>, even though it completes last.
</p>

<div class="flow">
  OTHER PEOPLE'S CLOCK — start day 1, finishes weeks later ├─ trademark clearance §5, decision 1 ├─
  counsel engagement + the brief §5, decision 3 ├─ independent security review ── book it now, run
  it week 6 └─ accessibility review with disabled users ── recruit now, run it week 7 YOUR CLOCK —
  start week 2, you control the pace ├─ production authentication ├─ connect the eight integrations
  that never ran ├─ encryption, scanning, backups └─ hosting, monitoring, on-call THE MARKET'S CLOCK
  — starts only after the launch gate in §7 └─ the first ten families §8
</div>

<div class="callout danger">
  <span class="label">The single hardest rule in this document</span>
  <p>
    <strong>No real person's memories enter the system until every box in §7 is ticked.</strong> Not
    a friendly beta family, not your own grandmother, not &ldquo;just to test with something
    real&rdquo;. The moment real material is in there, you have obligations you cannot yet meet, and
    the first archive is exactly the one you will care most about having handled badly. Synthetic
    data is not a limitation during Horizon&nbsp;1; it is the point of Horizon&nbsp;1.
  </p>
</div>

<h3>Week by week</h3>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 12%">Week</th>
      <th style="width: 36%">What ships</th>
      <th>Why it is in this position</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>1</strong></td>
      <td>
        Start every external clock. Correct the pricing-page tense. Name the accountable person.
      </td>
      <td>These cost you hours and buy you weeks.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>2&ndash;3</strong></td>
      <td>
        <strong>Production authentication.</strong> OIDC or passkeys, MFA enrolment,
        <em>and password reset</em>.
      </td>
      <td>
        Blocking item&nbsp;4. Without it the product cannot be deployed at all &mdash;
        <code>AUTH_DRIVER=local</code> is refused in production by design. Password reset is not on
        the blocking list but a pilot without it generates a support crisis in week two.
        <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span>
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>3</strong></td>
      <td>
        <strong>Real secrets.</strong> Replace every development placeholder and move them into a
        secret manager.
      </td>
      <td>
        <code>SESSION_SECRET</code> and <code>STORAGE_SIGNING_SECRET</code> currently hold strings
        that literally read <code>dev-only-…-change-me</code>.
        <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span> Shipping either is a total compromise of sessions or of
        object URLs.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>3&ndash;4</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Run the eight integrations that have never executed.</strong></td>
      <td>
        Each is written and type-checked and unproven. Detailed below &mdash; this week also
        produces your real unit costs.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>4&ndash;5</strong></td>
      <td>
        <strong>Encryption at rest with a customer-managed key</strong>;
        <strong>a real malware scanner</strong>.
      </td>
      <td>
        Blocking items&nbsp;3 and&nbsp;5. Today anyone with database or backup access reads
        everything, and the local scanner catches a test file and a mismatched type &mdash; it is
        not an antivirus. <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span>
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>5</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Backups, and a restore you actually perform.</strong></td>
      <td>
        Blocking item&nbsp;6. Your own document says the recovery targets are
        <em>stated, not measured</em>. Restore into a clean environment and time it.
        <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span>
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>5&ndash;6</strong></td>
      <td>Hosting, deploy pipeline, monitoring, alerting, on-call. Instrument OpenTelemetry.</td>
      <td>
        It is configured and not instrumented, so today you would find out about an outage from a
        customer. <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span>
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>6</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Independent security review runs.</strong></td>
      <td>Blocking item&nbsp;2. The isolation is currently tested by the person who wrote it.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>7</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Accessibility review with disabled users.</strong></td>
      <td>
        Blocking item&nbsp;7. Zero automated violations is a floor. Your users skew old; some will
        have low vision, tremor, or hearing loss. This is a core-audience issue, not a compliance
        checkbox.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>8</strong></td>
      <td>Fix what the two reviews found. Run the §7 gate. Legal answers land.</td>
      <td>Reserve the week. Both reviews will find things.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<div class="page-break"></div>
<h3>The eight integrations, and what each one teaches you</h3>

<p>
  These are complete and were <strong>never executed</strong>, because nothing was reachable from
  the build environment. <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span> Run them in this order; each has a
  specific first thing to check, and two of them produce numbers you need for pricing.
</p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 22%">Integration</th>
      <th style="width: 40%">First thing to check</th>
      <th>What it produces</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Docker Compose</td>
      <td><code>docker compose up</code> &mdash; watch the migrate step</td>
      <td>Everything else depends on it</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>S3 or MinIO</td>
      <td>Upload, then a presigned download, then deletion</td>
      <td><strong>Your storage cost per GB</strong></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Redis</td>
      <td>That revocation clears keys across <em>two</em> API instances</td>
      <td>Proves consent revocation survives horizontal scaling</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>pgvector</td>
      <td>That its results match the portable path</td>
      <td>Retrieval quality parity</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Hosted speech-to-text</td>
      <td>That segment locators still point at real spans</td>
      <td>
        <strong>Your largest variable cost</strong> &mdash; the local adapter cannot recognise
        speech at all
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Hosted OCR</td>
      <td>Same &mdash; that locators survive</td>
      <td>Document handling becomes real</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Hosted composition</td>
      <td>That verification still drops unsupported claims</td>
      <td>Whether you need it at all &mdash; see below</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>SMTP</td>
      <td>That no memory content appears in a subject line</td>
      <td>The privacy rule most easily broken by a convenience change</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Stripe</td>
      <td>
        <code>verifyWebhook</code> returns <code>null</code> &mdash; wire signature verification
      </td>
      <td>The ability to be paid</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<div class="callout ok">
  <span class="label">A question worth asking before you spend on hosted composition</span>
  <p>
    Your local composer is extractive: it can quote and stitch retrieved passages and
    <em>structurally cannot originate a claim</em>. That is a weaker system that reads more plainly
    &mdash; and it is also a system in which fabrication is unavailable rather than merely rare.
    Before you switch to a hosted model, put both in front of five real people and find out whether
    they prefer the fluent one. If they do not, you have just removed a cost line, a dependency and
    a cross-border transfer problem in one decision. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
  </p>
</div>

<h3>Explicitly not now</h3>
<p>
  These are real gaps and they are not Horizon&nbsp;1. Scope discipline is most of what makes an
  eight-week plan finish in eight weeks.
</p>
<div class="kv">
  <div><span>Contributor review queue</span><span>defer &mdash; proposals are recorded</span></div>
  <div><span>Admin UI for incidents</span><span>defer &mdash; read-only list is enough</span></div>
  <div>
    <span>Embedding-model backfill script</span
    ><span>defer &mdash; needed only when you change models</span>
  </div>
  <div><span>Rendered ERD</span><span>defer &mdash; the text diagram is accurate</span></div>
  <div>
    <span>Notification scheduling</span><span>never, by design &mdash; see §3, problem 4</span>
  </div>
  <div><span>Second region</span><span>Horizon 3, once you have customers in one</span></div>
  <div>
    <span>The asking artifact (§3)</span
    ><span>Horizon 2 &mdash; it is a growth tool, not a launch blocker</span>
  </div>
</div>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/23-part2-d.html`

```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-7">7&nbsp;&nbsp;The launch gate</h2>

<p class="lede">
  One page. Print it. No real person's memories enter the system until every box is ticked and you
  have signed the bottom. If a box cannot be ticked, the answer is to fix it, not to add a caveat.
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">Legal and accountability</p>
<ul class="check">
  <li>
    Counsel has answered the §5 brief, and the consent copy, teach-back wording, terms and
    succession screen carry their approval
  </li>
  <li>
    A policy exists for third parties named inside memories, and it is implemented, not merely
    written
  </li>
  <li>
    An accountable person is named by name in the runbook, on the support page, and in the customer
    agreement
  </li>
  <li>The name is cleared, or a rename has been completed</li>
  <li>Nothing on the public site claims traction, customers or capability that does not exist</li>
</ul>

<p class="eyebrow">Security</p>
<ul class="check">
  <li>
    Production authentication works: no <code>AUTH_DRIVER=local</code>, MFA available, password
    reset working
  </li>
  <li>Every development secret has been replaced and lives in a secret manager</li>
  <li>Encryption at rest with a customer-managed key</li>
  <li>A real malware scanner is in the upload path</li>
  <li>
    An independent security review has been completed and its findings closed or explicitly accepted
    in writing
  </li>
</ul>

<p class="eyebrow">Operations</p>
<ul class="check">
  <li>Backups run, and a restore has been <em>performed</em> into a clean environment and timed</li>
  <li>
    A deletion has been performed end to end and verified against the database afterwards &mdash;
    not against the receipt
  </li>
  <li>Monitoring and alerting reach a human within minutes; that human has agreed to be reached</li>
  <li>Logs, error reports and support views have been inspected and contain no memory content</li>
  <li>All eight integrations have been executed, not merely deployed</li>
  <li>Billing works, including verified webhook signatures, and a refund has been tested</li>
</ul>

<p class="eyebrow">Product</p>
<ul class="check">
  <li>
    An accessibility review with disabled users has been completed and blocking findings fixed
  </li>
  <li>
    The interview capture path has been exercised by hand, on real hardware, by someone over seventy
  </li>
  <li>Export has been produced and opened without EverEcho present</li>
  <li>A written runbook exists for the death of a storyteller during the pilot (§18)</li>
  <li>Real unit costs are known, and the price covers them</li>
</ul>

<div class="callout danger">
  <span class="label">Sign it</span>
  <p style="margin-top: 3mm">
    I confirm that every box above is ticked, that I have personally verified the ones marked
    <em>performed</em> rather than accepting a report, and that I am the person accountable if this
    goes wrong.
  </p>
  <p style="margin-top: 6mm">
    Signed &nbsp;______________________________ &nbsp;&nbsp; Date &nbsp;________________
  </p>
</div>

<p class="footnote">
  This is not ceremony. The list contains four things that are routinely skipped &mdash; a rehearsed
  restore, a verified deletion, a log inspection, and an accessibility review with actual disabled
  people &mdash; and skipping any of them is invisible until the day it is catastrophic.
</p>

<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-8">8&nbsp;&nbsp;Horizon 2: the first ten families</h2>

<div class="horizon">
  <span class="h-n">Horizon 2</span>
  <span>Ten paying archives. Not a hundred. Not free ones.</span>
  <span class="h-when">Months 2&ndash;5</span>
</div>

<p class="lede">
  The purpose of this cohort is not revenue and not growth. It is to answer four questions that no
  amount of thinking will answer, and to produce the one asset that makes everything in Part IV
  easier.
</p>

<h3>The four questions</h3>
<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 6%"></th>
      <th style="width: 34%">Question</th>
      <th>How you will know</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Q1</strong></td>
      <td>Will anyone pay, at a price that works?</td>
      <td>
        Ten families pay the §5 provisional price without a discount. If you had to discount, the
        answer is no and you have learned it cheaply.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Q2</strong></td>
      <td>Will the storyteller actually do the work?</td>
      <td>
        Payment &rarr; consent &rarr; first recording &rarr; <strong>first approved memory</strong>.
        Measure the drop at each step. This is the split-incentive problem from §3 meeting reality.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Q3</strong></td>
      <td>What does one archive really cost to serve?</td>
      <td>
        Every hour you spend, logged. Every provider invoice, attributed. Fill in the §2 worksheet
        with real numbers.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Q4</strong></td>
      <td>Does the refusal actually sell, or merely survive?</td>
      <td>
        Watch what people react to. If nobody mentions the citations or the abstention, your
        positioning is a private conviction rather than a market position &mdash; and §10 changes.
      </td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<h3>How to find ten families</h3>
<p>
  Do not run advertising. At ten units, paid acquisition teaches you nothing and costs you focus. Go
  where the occasion already lives (§3, problem 3):
</p>
<ol class="runbook">
  <li>
    <strong>Your own circle first, but paying.</strong> Friends and family who pay full price are a
    real signal; ones you comp are a favour, and favours produce polite feedback that will mislead
    you for months.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>One channel partner, unpaid pilot.</strong> A single estate planner, hospice,
    senior-living director or community organiser who will introduce you to three or four families.
    One partner, not five &mdash; you are testing whether the channel works, not building a channel
    programme.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>A community with a reason.</strong> Diaspora and migration communities have an unusually
    strong version of this need: the generation that moved is ageing, and the story of
    <em>why</em> they moved is exactly what is lost first. Your own demonstration archive is built
    around precisely that. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Do the interviews yourself.</strong> All ten. This is the concierge phase from §2 and it
    is deliberately unscalable. You are writing the specification for what the product must
    eventually automate, and you cannot write it from a desk.
  </li>
</ol>

<div class="callout warn">
  <span class="label">Two rules for this cohort</span>
  <p>
    <strong>Nobody gets it free.</strong> A free archive answers none of the four questions.<br />
    <strong>Nobody gets a discount to close.</strong> A discount converts Q1 from a measurement into
    a wish.
  </p>
</div>

<h3>What would falsify the idea</h3>
<p>
  Decide these thresholds <em>now</em>, before you are emotionally invested in ten specific
  families. Write them down and date them.
</p>
<div class="kv">
  <div>
    <span>Fewer than 5 of 10 reach a first approved memory</span
    ><span>the split-incentive problem is fatal as designed</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Cost to serve exceeds price, and is not obviously automatable</span
    ><span>the business does not work at this price</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Nobody mentions citation or refusal, unprompted</span
    ><span>reposition; the wedge is yours, not theirs</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>You cannot recruit 10 without paid acquisition</span
    ><span>the channel thesis in §10 is wrong</span>
  </div>
</div>

<p style="margin-top: 4mm">
  None of these means stop. Each means <em>change something specific</em>, and knowing which is
  worth more than the ten customers.
</p>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/30-part3-a.html`

```html
<div class="part-divider">
  <div class="kicker">Part III</div>
  <h2>Building the business</h2>
  <p>
    Price, channel, growth, measurement and team &mdash; the five things that turn ten families into
    a company.
  </p>
</div>

<h2 id="sec-9">9&nbsp;&nbsp;Pricing and the business model</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Section 2 established the constraint: a cheap price forecloses the outcome. This section turns
  that into a structure you can put on a page.
</p>

<h3>Price the occasion, not the software</h3>
<p>
  Cost-plus pricing will produce a small number, because your marginal costs are genuinely low. Do
  not price that way. Ask instead what a family already spends at this moment in their lives &mdash;
  a professional photographer for a milestone celebration, an hour with an estate lawyer, a
  headstone, a funeral. Those are the anchors your buyer is actually holding, and they are all far
  above what a software subscription would suggest. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
</p>

<h3>The structure I would use</h3>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 22%">Component</th>
      <th style="width: 16%">Shape</th>
      <th>What it is for</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Capture</strong></td>
      <td>One-time, large</td>
      <td>
        The guided interviews, the transcription, the structuring, the first biography draft, and
        the handholding. This is where the real work and the real cost sit, and where the value is
        most legible to the buyer.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Preservation</strong></td>
      <td>Annual, modest</td>
      <td>
        Storage, backups, keeping it reachable, keeping it exportable. Recurring because the
        obligation is recurring.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Family access</strong></td>
      <td>Included, unlimited</td>
      <td>
        <strong>Never charge per seat.</strong> Every additional family member increases the value,
        deepens retention (§3, problem 4) and costs almost nothing. Charging for them is the single
        most self-defeating pricing choice available to you.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Additional chapters</strong></td>
      <td>One-time, smaller</td>
      <td>
        Years later, more sessions. Offered only when the family asks &mdash; never prompted, per
        §3.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Long-term preservation</strong></td>
      <td>Optional prepay</td>
      <td>
        A stated term paid up front. Attractive to buyers, and dangerous to you &mdash; see the
        warning below.
      </td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<p>
  As a starting heuristic, not a market observation: set <strong>capture</strong> in the band a
  family would pay a good professional for a day's work plus a deliverable, and set
  <strong>annual preservation</strong> at roughly a tenth to a fifth of that. That shape puts you in
  model&nbsp;C of §2 without any heroic assumptions.
  <span class="ev a">ASSUMPTION &mdash; validate in §8, cohort of ten</span>
</p>

<div class="callout danger">
  <span class="label">Before you sell any prepaid preservation term</span>
  <p>
    A one-time payment for long-term storage is revenue today and an obligation for decades. Three
    things must be true first: counsel has answered whether it creates trust, escrow or reserve
    obligations (§5, brief item 11); you have real storage costs from Horizon&nbsp;1; and the term
    is <strong>stated in years</strong>, not described as &ldquo;forever&rdquo;. Never write the
    word forever on a pricing page. You cannot promise it, and the one thing this company cannot
    afford is a promise it cannot keep.
  </p>
</div>

<h3>Decide the non-payment policy now, and publish it</h3>
<p>
  A family will stop paying. Perhaps they cannot afford it; perhaps the storyteller has died and
  nobody feels able to make the decision. What happens to the archive is a question you must answer
  <em>before</em> anyone pays, in plain words, on the pricing page.
</p>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision &mdash; what lapse means</span>
  <p>
    The options are: delete after notice; freeze and retain read-only; retain fully at your cost; or
    export-and-close.
  </p>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>Recommendation:</strong> a long grace period, then
    <strong>export-and-close</strong> &mdash; you generate the full export, deliver it, confirm
    receipt, and then delete on a stated schedule. It keeps your storage liability bounded, it holds
    nothing hostage, and it is consistent with everything else the product promises. Your
    shutdown-and-portability commitments already point this way; make it the individual-account
    policy too.
  </p>
</div>

<h3>Things you must never do, for money</h3>
<div class="kv">
  <div>
    <span>Advertising against memories</span
    ><span>prohibited &mdash; and would end the company</span>
  </div>
  <div><span>Selling or brokering data</span><span>prohibited</span></div>
  <div>
    <span>Training shared models on private archives</span
    ><span>prohibited &mdash; refused by the policy compiler</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Charging per question asked</span
    ><span>perverse: it prices curiosity and rewards fluent guessing</span>
  </div>
  <div><span>Engagement-based pricing</span><span>directly contradicts §3, problem 4</span></div>
  <div><span>Charging for export</span><span>the ability to leave must always be free</span></div>
  <div>
    <span>Charging per family member</span><span>taxes the thing that creates your retention</span>
  </div>
</div>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/31-part3-b.html`

```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-10">10&nbsp;&nbsp;The channel question</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Section 3 concluded that you cannot manufacture the occasion, so you must attach to people who
  already own it. This section says which people, in what order, and how to test one without
  committing to all of them.
</p>

<h3>What makes a channel good, for this product specifically</h3>
<div class="kv">
  <div><span>Owns the moment</span><span>is already present at a trigger event</span></div>
  <div><span>Holds the trust</span><span>the family already takes their advice</span></div>
  <div>
    <span>Cannot touch simulation</span><span>your refusal is a requirement, not a quirk</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Reaches the storyteller, not only the buyer</span><span>solves §3, problem 2</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Has a budget or a fee relationship</span
    ><span>can transact without a new purchase decision</span>
  </div>
</div>

<h3>The candidates, ranked</h3>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 5%"></th>
      <th style="width: 22%">Channel</th>
      <th style="width: 34%">Why it fits</th>
      <th>The problem with it</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>1</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Estate, will and private-client advisers</strong></td>
      <td>
        Present at exactly the moment a person is thinking about what they leave behind. High-trust,
        fee-based, used to handling sensitive family material. Clients skew to the right age and
        means.
      </td>
      <td>
        Slow, relationship-driven sales. They will not risk their client relationship on an unproven
        vendor &mdash; which is precisely what §4's readiness document is for.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>2</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Senior living communities</strong></td>
      <td>
        Concentrated population, an activities budget, staff whose job is meaningful engagement, and
        a recurring institutional relationship rather than one family at a time.
      </td>
      <td>
        Institutional procurement. Consent gets complicated when a facility introduces the service
        &mdash; the storyteller must still be the one who decides, and you must design so that it
        visibly is.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>3</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Hospice and palliative care</strong></td>
      <td>
        The most acute version of the need; legacy work is already part of good practice. Deeply
        values the refusal &mdash; no hospice can be near a simulation product.
      </td>
      <td>
        The hardest possible operating conditions: little time, fragile participants, and a cohort
        where death during the engagement is not a risk but an expectation. Do not start here. Earn
        it.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>4</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Diaspora and community organisations</strong></td>
      <td>
        An unusually strong version of the need &mdash; the generation that migrated is ageing, and
        the reason they left is the first thing lost. Trusted community intermediaries; natural word
        of mouth.
      </td>
      <td>
        Fragmented, often unfunded, and the buyer may be the community rather than the family. Test
        as a source of families, not as a revenue channel.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>5</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Archives, museums, universities</strong></td>
      <td>
        Oral-history practice already exists, with real methodology you can learn from. Budget for
        provenance and rights management. Values citation natively.
      </td>
      <td>
        This is a different product with a different buyer, and it pulls you toward §4's
        infrastructure fork. Genuinely promising; a distraction before month twelve.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>6</strong></td>
      <td>Direct consumer advertising</td>
      <td>Fast to start.</td>
      <td>
        Low intent, split incentive, no occasion, delayed verdict. Every structural problem in §3 is
        at its worst here. <strong>Not recommended before you have a proven channel.</strong>
      </td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision &mdash; which one to test first</span>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>Recommendation: estate and private-client advisers, one partner, during §8.</strong>
    They combine trust, an owned occasion, a transacting relationship and a client base that can pay
    a model&#8209;C price. Senior living is the strong second and a better fit if your first ten
    families come through one. Hospice is where this product may matter most and it is the last one
    you should attempt, not the first &mdash; go there when your operations are boring and your
    death runbook has been used.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="page-break"></div>
<h3>How to test a channel without building a channel programme</h3>
<ol class="runbook">
  <li>
    <strong>One partner. One.</strong> Five partners produce five weak relationships and no signal.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Ask for introductions, not a contract.</strong> Three or four families is a complete
    test. Revenue share and paperwork can wait until you know it works.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Give them the readiness document unprompted.</strong> Their real question is what
    happens to their reputation if this goes wrong. Answering it before they ask is the fastest
    trust you will ever buy.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Watch who actually does the asking.</strong> If the adviser will not raise it with a
    client, the channel is dead however enthusiastic they were in the meeting. Enthusiasm is not
    distribution.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Instrument it:</strong> introductions made, families who took a call, families who paid,
    families who reached a first approved memory. Four numbers. If introductions are high and calls
    are low, your asking artifact is weak. If calls are high and payment is low, your price or your
    proof is wrong.
  </li>
</ol>

<div class="callout warn">
  <span class="label">The consent trap in every institutional channel</span>
  <p>
    When a facility, an adviser or a hospice introduces the service, there is a structural risk that
    the storyteller feels the decision has already been made for them by someone with authority over
    their care or their money. Your product refuses to proceed without them &mdash; but refusing is
    not enough if the person feels obliged.
  </p>
  <p>
    Design against it explicitly: the storyteller's consent conversation happens
    <strong>without the introducing party present</strong>, declining is unremarkable and costs the
    family nothing, and the partner is never told why an archive did not proceed. Write this into
    the partner agreement. It will lose you a small amount of revenue and it is not negotiable
    &mdash; a consent obtained under institutional pressure is the exact failure this entire product
    exists to prevent. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
  </p>
</div>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/32-part3-c.html`

```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-11">11&nbsp;&nbsp;Growth without breaking your own rules</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Most growth playbooks are unavailable to you, and not by accident &mdash; you removed them on
  purpose. This section says exactly what is closed, what remains, and why what remains is unusually
  strong.
</p>

<h3>What is closed to you</h3>
<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 34%">Standard tactic</th>
      <th>Why you cannot use it</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>Content-based targeting and retargeting</td>
      <td>
        Memory content may never reach analytics. The constraint is enforced in the code that builds
        each event, not left to discipline. <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span>
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Engagement email, digests, streaks, reminders</td>
      <td>
        There is no notification scheduler, deliberately. Reminders about a parent's mortality
        become guilt with almost no effort. <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span>
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Rich behavioural analytics from third-party SDKs</td>
      <td>
        Most consumer analytics tooling assumes it may see page content. Yours may not. Expect to
        build a small amount of first-party measurement instead.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Testimonials quoting real memories</td>
      <td>
        Possible, but only under a separate, explicit, revocable marketing consent that is never a
        condition of service and never bundled into the main flow. Treat every such quote as
        borrowed, not owned.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Referral mechanics with social pressure</td>
      <td>
        &ldquo;Invite your siblings before it's too late&rdquo; is precisely the guilt loop the
        product prohibits.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>Urgency and scarcity marketing</td>
      <td>The honest version of urgency here is a person's death. Do not go near it.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<h3>What remains &mdash; and it is better than what you gave up</h3>

<p class="eyebrow">1. Give away the questions</p>
<p>
  The interview question set is your most valuable and least protectable asset, and §3 established
  that <em>interview quality is the actual product</em>. Publish it: a free, beautiful, genuinely
  useful guide to interviewing your own parents, with no product requirement at all. Most people who
  download it will do nothing, some will try and discover how hard it is to do well, and a few will
  come back and pay you to do it properly. It costs nothing, it is honest, it demonstrates expertise
  better than any claim, and it is the single best top-of-funnel asset available to this business.
  <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">2. Publish the readiness document</p>
<p>
  As argued in §4. Radical transparency about your own gaps is both a trust asset and a story
  journalists will actually run, because almost nobody does it.
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">3. Be the contrasting quote</p>
<p>
  Stories about AI resurrection products appear regularly, and every one needs someone credible to
  say what the responsible version looks like. That person can be you, and it costs you nothing but
  availability. Write the position clearly once, keep it current, and be easy to reach.
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">4. The asking artifact</p>
<p>
  From §3, problem 2 &mdash; the letter or page a child gives a parent. It is a product feature and
  a growth mechanism at once, because it travels between exactly the two people who must both agree.
  It does not exist yet. Build it in Horizon&nbsp;2.
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">5. The physical deliverable</p>
<p>
  The printed biography draft is a marketing object that sits on a table and gets picked up by
  visitors. In a category with a delayed verdict (§3, problem 5), a tangible artefact is how you get
  word of mouth a decade before the archive is truly needed.
</p>

<p class="eyebrow">6. Informational search</p>
<p>
  People search for how to record a parent's stories, what to ask a grandparent, how to preserve old
  photographs. Those searches are the closest thing this category has to declared intent, and
  answering them well is a durable asset that does not require you to say anything untrue.
</p>

<div class="callout ok">
  <span class="label">The pattern</span>
  <p>
    Every channel that remains open to you works by
    <strong>being genuinely useful before anyone pays</strong>, rather than by manufacturing
    pressure. That is slower. It is also the only kind of growth that is consistent with the
    product, and consistency here is not a nicety &mdash; the moment your marketing behaves
    differently from your product, the trust that is your entire differentiator is gone, and it does
    not come back.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-12">12&nbsp;&nbsp;The metrics that matter</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Fewer than you think, and several of them are unusual. Two of the standard ones will actively
  mislead you if you track them.
</p>

<h3>The five that decide whether this works</h3>
<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 30%">Metric</th>
      <th style="width: 36%">Definition</th>
      <th>Why</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Time to first approved memory</strong></td>
      <td>Payment &rarr; the storyteller approving their first memory</td>
      <td>
        Your true activation event. Everything before it is a promise; this is the moment the
        product has done something. Directly measures §3, problem 2.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Archive completeness</strong></td>
      <td>Decades, relationships and themes covered versus a target shape</td>
      <td>
        The only early proxy for a verdict that otherwise arrives years late (§3, problem 5). Turns
        an unmeasurable outcome into a visible gap.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Members per archive</strong></td>
      <td>People with active access</td>
      <td>Your real retention driver. Each additional member makes cancelling less thinkable.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Gross margin, per cohort</strong></td>
      <td>Revenue minus cost to serve, by month of joining</td>
      <td>
        The alarm for the §2 margin trap. If cohort margin is not improving as you automate,
        concierge has quietly become the company.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Twelve-month retention</strong></td>
      <td>Archives still paying after a year</td>
      <td>
        The only retention number that means anything for a custody product. Measure it annually; do
        not infer it from monthly activity.
      </td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<h3>Two that are specific to what you built</h3>
<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 30%">Metric</th>
      <th>What it tells you</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>
        <strong>Abstention rate</strong><br /><span class="footnote"
          >questions answered with the refusal sentence</span
        >
      </td>
      <td>
        A health metric with a <em>band</em>, not a target. Too low and something is answering
        things it should not &mdash; check verification. Too high and either the archive is too thin
        (a completeness problem, tell the family) or retrieval has broken (an engineering problem).
        Alert on movement in either direction; a sudden drop is the most dangerous signal this
        system can produce.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>Consent narrowing and revocation rate</strong></td>
      <td>
        People tightening their permissions is a trust signal in reverse. A rise means something in
        the product, the marketing or a partner made someone uncomfortable. Read the audit log, do
        not just count.
      </td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<h3>Do not track these</h3>
<div class="kv">
  <div>
    <span>Daily or monthly active users</span
    ><span>a finished archive is unopened by design; this number will panic you over nothing</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Session length, time in app</span
    ><span>optimising it means manufacturing engagement, which is prohibited</span>
  </div>
  <div><span>Questions asked per week</span><span>same trap, and it prices curiosity</span></div>
  <div>
    <span>Net promoter score in year one</span
    ><span>the verdict arrives years late; you would be measuring politeness</span>
  </div>
</div>

<p style="margin-top: 4mm" class="footnote">
  All of the above must be computed without memory content ever reaching an analytics store &mdash;
  which is achievable for every metric listed, and is the reason none of them requires knowing what
  any archive contains.
</p>
```
