```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-13">13&nbsp;&nbsp;The team, in hiring order</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Five roles, each with the trigger that says it is time. Hiring before the trigger burns money you
  do not have; hiring after it means you have already been the bottleneck for a month.
</p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 6%"></th>
      <th style="width: 26%">Role</th>
      <th style="width: 30%">Hire when</th>
      <th>Why this order</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>1</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Interviewer / storyteller success</strong></td>
      <td>
        You are conducting more than about six interviews a month, or interviews are being scheduled
        around your availability
      </td>
      <td>
        Interview quality <em>is</em> the product (§3, problem 5), and it is the first thing that
        breaks when you get busy. Hire for warmth and curiosity, not for technology &mdash; oral
        history, journalism, social work, chaplaincy and teaching all produce good candidates.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>2</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Engineer</strong></td>
      <td>You are choosing between shipping and selling in the same week, more than once</td>
      <td>
        Everything is TypeScript with no build step and 279 passing tests, so a competent engineer
        is productive quickly. Have them start by taking the deployment and on-call, which is the
        work that most fragments a founder's attention.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>3</strong></td>
      <td>
        <strong>Privacy and legal operations</strong><br /><span class="footnote"
          >fractional first</span
        >
      </td>
      <td>
        A second jurisdiction, a first institutional contract, or the first data-subject request
        from someone who is not a customer
      </td>
      <td>
        The third-party-in-memories question (§5, brief item 4) will generate real operational work.
        Fractional is right until it isn't; the trigger for full-time is a second regulator.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>4</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Partnerships</strong></td>
      <td>
        One channel has produced families twice, repeatably, without you personally in the room
      </td>
      <td>
        Hiring this before the channel is proven means paying someone to discover that your thesis
        was wrong &mdash; which you can discover yourself for free in §8 and §10.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>5</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Support lead</strong></td>
      <td>
        Support minutes per archive &times; live archives exceeds what one person can absorb
        alongside another job
      </td>
      <td>
        See the warning below. This is not a normal support hire and staffing it like one will hurt
        someone.
      </td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<div class="callout warn">
  <span class="label">Support here is not normal support</span>
  <p>
    Your support inbox will contain a message from someone whose parent died last week asking why a
    recording will not play. It will contain families in conflict about who may see what. It will
    contain a person who wants to delete everything, at midnight, and means it.
  </p>
  <p>
    Staff this deliberately: written escalation paths, a hard rule that nobody handles these alone,
    access to actual supervision, and a workload that assumes emotional labour rather than ticket
    throughput. And note the constraint you built &mdash; the support view shows operational
    metadata only, never memory content &mdash; which is right, and which means your support people
    will sometimes be helping with something they cannot see. Train for that explicitly.
    <span class="ev v">VERIFIED &mdash; scope is metadata-only in code</span>
  </p>
</div>

<h3>Who not to hire, and when not to</h3>
<div class="kv">
  <div>
    <span>A growth marketer, early</span
    ><span
      >most of the standard playbook is closed to you (§11); they will be frustrated and you will
      waste the hire</span
    >
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>A salesperson before the channel is proven</span><span>see role 4's trigger</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>An AI/ML specialist</span
    ><span
      >the retrieval and verification are done and deliberately conservative; there is no model
      problem to solve yet</span
    >
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>A designer, full-time, early</span
    ><span
      >the interface is built and passes accessibility; use contract design for the asking artifact
      and the printed deliverable</span
    >
  </div>
</div>

<h3>The one thing you should not delegate</h3>
<p>
  Conduct interviews yourself for longer than is comfortable &mdash; well past the first ten. It is
  the only place where you learn what the product must become, and it is the first thing every
  founder in your position hands off, because it does not feel like work on the company. It is the
  work on the company.
</p>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/40-part4-a.html`

```html
<div class="part-divider">
  <div class="kicker">Part IV</div>
  <h2>Money</h2>
  <p>
    Whether to raise it, how to raise it if you do, and the staged path the arithmetic in §2
    actually implies.
  </p>
</div>

<h2 id="sec-14">14&nbsp;&nbsp;Bootstrap or raise</h2>

<p class="lede">
  The generic answer is &ldquo;raise, because you want a large outcome.&rdquo; For this business the
  generic answer is wrong about the timing and right about the destination.
</p>

<h3>The case for not raising yet</h3>
<ul>
  <li>
    <strong>Nothing is racing you.</strong> There is no network effect, no land grab, no
    winner-take-all dynamic. Nobody wins this market by being six months earlier; they win it by
    being trusted, and trust does not respond to capital.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>The concierge phase earns money from the first customer.</strong> Model&nbsp;C pricing
    on ten families is real revenue during the period you would otherwise be fundraising.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Capital creates pressure toward exactly the features you have prohibited.</strong> A
    board watching flat engagement will, sincerely and reasonably, ask why you will not add the
    voice. Every prohibition in this product is a growth constraint, which is the whole point, and
    money makes constraints feel like problems.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>You have no answer yet to the questions money would make urgent.</strong> Raising before
    §8 means spending someone else's money to discover your price and your channel &mdash; which you
    can discover for far less.
  </li>
</ul>

<h3>The case for raising</h3>
<ul>
  <li>
    <strong>You asked for a billion-dollar outcome.</strong> Reaching $100M of recurring revenue
    without external capital is rare enough that planning for it would be planning on an exception.
    <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>The launch gate costs real money.</strong> An independent security review, counsel in
    multiple jurisdictions, encryption infrastructure, a real scanner and hosting are not small
    sums, and none of them is optional.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Channel sales cycles are long.</strong> Estate advisers and senior-living operators move
    over quarters. That requires runway, not hustle.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Preservation is a balance-sheet promise.</strong> Committing to hold something for
    decades is more credible from a company with capital than from one person with a card.
  </li>
</ul>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision &mdash; the sequence I recommend</span>
  <p>
    <strong
      >Bootstrap through §8. Then raise a small round on the strength of ten paying
      families.</strong
    >
  </p>
  <p>
    Ten families who paid full price, with a measured cost to serve, a real activation rate and one
    channel that produced introductions, is a stronger fundraising asset than any deck you could
    write instead &mdash; and it costs you three months rather than three months of meetings. It
    also inverts the power in the conversation, which matters enormously for the next point.
  </p>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>And the part almost nobody plans:</strong> choose investors by whether they will accept
    the §17 governance terms in writing. An investor who treats the prohibitions as a phase is not a
    cheaper investor &mdash; they are a future fight over the thing your company exists to be. Raise
    less, from people who understand what they are funding.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-15">15&nbsp;&nbsp;If you raise</h2>

<h3>The narrative</h3>
<p>
  Do not lead with the family archive. Lead with the thesis, because the thesis is what makes the
  archive interesting:
</p>

<div class="callout">
  <p style="font-size: 11.5pt; font-family: Georgia, serif; margin-bottom: 2mm">
    &ldquo;The industry is racing to simulate dead people. That is going to fail publicly and badly,
    and when it does, every serious institution &mdash; every hospice, university, bank and family
    &mdash; will need the version that refuses. We built that version first, and the hard part is
    not the product. It is the consent and provenance machinery underneath it, which took eight
    months and which nobody copies in a quarter.&rdquo;
  </p>
</div>

<h3>The order to present in</h3>
<ol class="runbook">
  <li>
    The problem, told through the failure mode: a grieving family believing a fabricated answer.
  </li>
  <li>The refusal, as a position rather than a policy &mdash; and the demo pair from §3, live.</li>
  <li>
    What is actually built: 279 tests, forced isolation, 100% claim-to-citation, zero permission
    leaks, all measured.
  </li>
  <li>The ten families: price paid, activation rate, cost to serve, channel origin.</li>
  <li>Why the machinery is the moat, and the optionality in §4.</li>
  <li>The channel thesis, with the one partner that worked.</li>
  <li>
    The arithmetic from §2, honestly &mdash; including why you are not building a cheap consumer
    subscription.
  </li>
  <li>The readiness document, handed over unprompted.</li>
  <li>What the money buys, tied to the §16 stage you are trying to reach.</li>
</ol>

<h3>What you will be asked, and what is actually true</h3>
<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 36%">The question</th>
      <th>The honest answer</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><em>&ldquo;Why not add voice cloning? Users will want it.&rdquo;</em></td>
      <td>
        The one that matters. Answer: because the archive is only worth filling if the storyteller
        believes it will never be used that way, and a company that would add it later is one they
        must reason about today. Then point out that it is refused by a policy compiler and a test,
        not by a promise &mdash; which is why institutions can buy it.
        <strong>Prepare this answer word for word.</strong> You will give it in every meeting.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><em>&ldquo;Isn't the market small?&rdquo;</em></td>
      <td>
        Show §2. The answer is not that the market is large; it is that revenue per archive can be
        large, and here is the price ten families actually paid.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><em>&ldquo;What's your CAC?&rdquo;</em></td>
      <td>
        <span class="ev u">UNKNOWN</span>, and say so. Then say precisely how you will find out and
        by when. A founder who says &ldquo;I don't know yet, here's the experiment&rdquo; is more
        credible than one with a confident invented number &mdash; and this is a company whose
        entire pitch is not inventing numbers.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><em>&ldquo;Why won't they churn once the archive is finished?&rdquo;</em></td>
      <td>
        Custody, not engagement (§3, problem 4). Members per archive is the retention driver. Be
        honest that twelve-month retention is not yet measured.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><em>&ldquo;Why can't a large platform do this tomorrow?&rdquo;</em></td>
      <td>
        They can build the features. What they will not do is adopt the refusal, because it is
        directly opposed to their engagement and data incentives &mdash; and without the refusal,
        the product is the thing you are not.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><em>&ldquo;What happens when someone dies?&rdquo;</em></td>
      <td>
        Answer operationally, not philosophically: the succession directive, the runbook, and the
        honest note that no automatic transition can ever be triggered by inactivity.
      </td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<h3>Where you will be attacked, fairly</h3>
<div class="kv">
  <div>
    <span>Services margin inside model C</span
    ><span>answer with the cohort margin trend from §12</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Perpetual storage liability</span
    ><span>answer with the §9 policy and the stated term</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Category contamination with griefbots</span
    ><span>answer by making it your acquisition channel</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>No traction</span><span>answer with ten paying families and the readiness document</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Single founder, if you are one</span><span>answer with the hiring triggers in §13</span>
  </div>
</div>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/41-part4-b.html`

```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-16">16&nbsp;&nbsp;The staged path to scale</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Five stages. Each has one thing that must become true before the next is attempted, and a branch
  point where the honest answer might be to change direction rather than push harder.
</p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 8%">Stage</th>
      <th style="width: 14%">Archives</th>
      <th style="width: 14%">Roughly</th>
      <th style="width: 32%">What must become true</th>
      <th>Branch if it doesn't</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>0</strong></td>
      <td class="t-num">10</td>
      <td>Month 5</td>
      <td>People pay full price and storytellers reach a first approved memory</td>
      <td>Reprice, or fix activation. Do not proceed on hope.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>1</strong></td>
      <td class="t-num">100</td>
      <td>Year 1</td>
      <td>
        <strong>One channel produces families repeatably without you in the room.</strong> Capture
        is partly productised. Cohort margin is rising.
      </td>
      <td>
        Try the second channel in §10. If two fail, the channel thesis is wrong and consumer-direct
        must be tested properly.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>2</strong></td>
      <td class="t-num">1,000</td>
      <td>Year 2&ndash;3</td>
      <td>
        Gross margin approaching software rather than services. Interviewers are hired and trained,
        not you. Twelve-month retention measured and acceptable.
      </td>
      <td>
        <strong>The real branch point.</strong> If margin is stuck, this is a services business
        &mdash; a good one, but not the §2 outcome. Decide deliberately whether that is acceptable.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>3</strong></td>
      <td class="t-num">10,000</td>
      <td>Year 4&ndash;5</td>
      <td>
        Multiple channels. Institutional accounts (model&nbsp;D) contributing. Operations boring
        enough to survive a bad week.
      </td>
      <td>
        If consumer stalls but institutions pull, follow the pull &mdash; that is the §4
        infrastructure fork opening legitimately.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>4</strong></td>
      <td class="t-num">50,000</td>
      <td>Year 6&ndash;7</td>
      <td>
        Model&nbsp;C revenue per archive sustained at scale &rArr; approximately $100M ARR &rArr;
        the §2 arithmetic.
      </td>
      <td>&mdash;</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<h3>What that growth rate actually means</h3>
<div class="arith">
  <div class="r"><span>From</span><span>10 archives</span></div>
  <div class="r"><span>To</span><span>50,000 archives</span></div>
  <div class="r"><span>Over</span><span>~6 years</span></div>
  <div class="r tot">
    <span>Sustained annual growth required</span><span>~4&times; per year</span>
  </div>
</div>

<p>
  Sustaining roughly four-fold growth for six consecutive years is the shape of companies that reach
  this outcome. It is also where most attempts stop &mdash; typically between stages&nbsp;2
  and&nbsp;3, when the founder-led magic stops working and the machine that replaces it has not been
  built. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
</p>

<div class="callout warn">
  <span class="label">The stage-2 to stage-3 transition is the whole game</span>
  <p>
    Everything before stage&nbsp;2 you can do through effort and taste. Everything after it requires
    that the quality of an interview does not depend on you being in the room. That is a training,
    tooling and standards problem, and it is the one to start solving at stage&nbsp;1 &mdash; a year
    before you need it &mdash; because founders who wait until they feel the pain take eighteen
    months to recover from it.
  </p>
</div>

<h3>Two honest observations about this table</h3>
<p>
  <strong>First:</strong> stages 0 and 1 are things I would bet on. Stage 2 is genuinely uncertain
  and depends on a margin question nobody can answer from here. Stages 3 and 4 are arithmetic, not
  forecasts &mdash; they describe what would have to happen, not what will.
</p>

<p>
  <strong>Second:</strong> stopping at stage 2 or 3 is not failure. A company with a thousand or ten
  thousand families, sound margins and an intact promise is a good outcome by any measure that is
  not this document's title. Keep that in view, because the arithmetic in §2 has a way of making a
  real business feel like a disappointment, and that feeling has ended more good companies than any
  competitor.
</p>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/50-part5-a.html`

```html
<div class="part-divider">
  <div class="kicker">Part V</div>
  <h2>Governance and risk</h2>
  <p>
    How to make the refusal survive you, what will actually go wrong, and the conditions under which
    I would tell you to stop.
  </p>
</div>

<h2 id="sec-17">17&nbsp;&nbsp;Binding the refusal so it survives you</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Today the prohibitions hold because you wrote them and you care. That is the weakest form of
  guarantee there is, and the whole product's value rests on it.
</p>

<h3>Why this is urgent rather than philosophical</h3>
<p>
  The pressure to add the voice will not arrive as a villain. It will arrive as a good person with a
  good argument at a bad moment: a board member after two flat quarters, an acquirer whose offer
  changes your family's life, a large customer who will sign if you add just one feature, or a
  grieving user who begs you for it. Every one of those is a sincere request, and the reason to
  decide now is that you will not be at your most clear-headed in any of those rooms.
</p>

<p>
  You already did the technical half: a policy compiler that refuses, a function that discards
  first-person output, database constraints, and tests that fail if any of it is removed.
  <span class="ev v">VERIFIED</span> But code is changed by whoever controls the company, and right
  now that protection is exactly as strong as your continued ownership.
</p>

<h3>The instruments, from cheapest to strongest</h3>
<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 6%"></th>
      <th style="width: 26%">Instrument</th>
      <th style="width: 36%">What it does</th>
      <th>Cost</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>1</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Publish the prohibitions as terms</strong></td>
      <td>
        Makes them a promise every customer can hold you to, not a marketing claim. Enforceable by
        the people they protect.
      </td>
      <td>A page and counsel's time. Do this before the first customer.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>2</strong></td>
      <td><strong>A purpose clause in the constitutional documents</strong></td>
      <td>
        Names the prohibited activities in the company's own governing document, so removing them is
        a formal act with a paper trail rather than a product decision.
      </td>
      <td>Incorporation-time work. Far harder to add later.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>3</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Reserved matters</strong></td>
      <td>
        Changing the prohibitions requires a supermajority or a specific consent, so no ordinary
        board majority can do it quietly.
      </td>
      <td>
        Must be negotiated <em>before</em> you take money, which is why §14 says choose investors on
        this.
      </td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>4</strong></td>
      <td><strong>An outside voice with a real veto</strong></td>
      <td>
        One or two independent people &mdash; an ethicist, a palliative-care clinician, an archivist
        &mdash; with a defined and narrow veto over the prohibited list. Not an advisory board;
        advisory boards advise.
      </td>
      <td>Modest fees, and the discipline of being argued with.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>5</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Change-of-control protections</strong></td>
      <td>
        On acquisition, the prohibitions survive, and every family gets notice plus a guaranteed
        window to export and delete. It makes the archives less useful to a buyer who wants them for
        the wrong reason &mdash; which is the point.
      </td>
      <td>Real. It may reduce your exit price, and that is the trade you are choosing.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td><strong>6</strong></td>
      <td><strong>Publish the enforcing tests</strong></td>
      <td>
        Anyone can verify the refusal is still enforced in the shipped product. Turns a claim into
        something falsifiable by strangers.
      </td>
      <td>Nearly free. Uniquely credible.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<div class="decision">
  <span class="d-label">Decision &mdash; how far to go</span>
  <p class="rec">
    <strong>Recommendation: do 1, 2 and 6 now</strong> &mdash; before the first customer and before
    incorporation is final, because two of them are much harder to retrofit.
    <strong>Negotiate 3 and 5 into the first round</strong> in §14.
    <strong>Add 4 at stage&nbsp;1</strong>, when there are real families whose interests deserve
    representation that is not you.
  </p>
</div>

<p>
  Instrument 5 is the one that will feel expensive, so be clear-eyed: you are deliberately lowering
  the value of an exit to a buyer whose plan is to remove the refusal. That is not a sacrifice made
  against your interest &mdash; it is the thing that makes the promise real, and the promise is the
  company.
</p>
```

```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-18">18&nbsp;&nbsp;The risk register</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Ranked by expected damage, not by how alarming they sound. The first one is not a risk &mdash; it
  is a certainty you are not yet prepared for.
</p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 5%">#</th>
      <th style="width: 26%">Risk</th>
      <th style="width: 11%">Likelihood</th>
      <th style="width: 29%">Mitigation</th>
      <th>Early warning</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>1</td>
      <td><strong>A storyteller dies mid-engagement</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge no">certain</span></td>
      <td>A written runbook, before the first family. See below.</td>
      <td>None. It simply happens.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>2</td>
      <td><strong>A family conflict over access</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge no">high</span></td>
      <td>
        The dispute-hold mechanism exists in the schema; write the human policy for who decides and
        on what evidence.
      </td>
      <td>Access requests from people the storyteller did not invite.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>3</td>
      <td><strong>A third party objects to appearing in a memory</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge partial">medium-high</span></td>
      <td>
        Counsel brief item 4; likely needs a redaction path and an objection route in product.
      </td>
      <td>The first such email. Do not improvise a reply.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>4</td>
      <td><strong>Cost to serve exceeds price</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge partial">medium-high</span></td>
      <td>Fill the §2 worksheet in Horizon 1; watch cohort margin monthly (§12).</td>
      <td>Cohort margin flat across three cohorts.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>5</td>
      <td><strong>Founder is the single point of failure</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge partial">medium-high</span></td>
      <td>
        Hiring triggers in §13; document operations as you go; the runbook must be usable by someone
        else.
      </td>
      <td>You have not taken a full week off, and cannot.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>6</td>
      <td><strong>A fabrication reaches a family and is believed</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge partial">low-medium</span></td>
      <td>
        Verification and third-person assertion already run on every answer; the abstention band in
        §12 is the alarm.
      </td>
      <td>Abstention rate falls without an obvious cause. Treat as an incident.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>7</td>
      <td><strong>A breach</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge partial">low-medium</span></td>
      <td>
        The launch gate; encryption with a customer-managed key; independent review; forced
        isolation already in place.
      </td>
      <td>Anything anomalous in the audit trail. Read it weekly (§20).</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>8</td>
      <td><strong>A channel partner pressures a storyteller</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge partial">medium</span></td>
      <td>
        The partner-agreement rules in §10 &mdash; consent conversation without the partner present,
        declining is costless, no feedback on why.
      </td>
      <td>A rise in consent narrowing or revocation from one partner's families (§12).</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>9</td>
      <td><strong>Acquisition or investor pressure to remove the refusal</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge partial">medium</span></td>
      <td>Every instrument in §17. This is what they are for.</td>
      <td>The first time you hear yourself say &ldquo;maybe just for enterprise&rdquo;.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>10</td>
      <td><strong>Provider dependency</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge partial">medium</span></td>
      <td>
        Every provider sits behind an adapter with a working local implementation &mdash; this risk
        is already largely engineered away. Keep it that way.
      </td>
      <td>A pricing change email from a speech-to-text vendor.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>11</td>
      <td><strong>Reputational contamination with griefbots</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge partial">medium</span></td>
      <td>§4 and §11 &mdash; own the distinction loudly and early.</td>
      <td>Being described as one, in writing, by someone who read your site.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>12</td>
      <td><strong>Regulatory action</strong></td>
      <td><span class="badge done">low, if §5 is done</span></td>
      <td>The counsel brief, honestly answered and implemented.</td>
      <td>A data-subject request you do not know how to answer.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<div class="callout danger">
  <span class="label">Risk 1 in full: write this runbook before the first family</span>
  <p>
    Your product is for older people, and you will be working with a cohort of them for months.
    <strong>Someone in your first fifty families will die during the engagement.</strong> This is
    not a risk to be mitigated; it is a scheduled event whose date is unknown.
  </p>
  <p>What must be decided in advance, in writing, while it is still abstract:</p>
  <ul style="margin-top: 2mm">
    <li>How you find out, and who tells you.</li>
    <li>
      What happens to a half-finished archive &mdash; recordings not yet transcribed, memories not
      yet approved.
      <strong>Nobody but the storyteller can approve them, and the storyteller is gone.</strong>
      Decide now what unapproved material means after death. This is the hardest question in the
      product and it has no default answer.
    </li>
    <li>Who may act: the succession directive, if one exists, and what happens if it does not.</li>
    <li>What you send the family, and when. Not a system email. A person.</li>
    <li>
      Billing: suspended immediately, no renewal notice, no dunning. Check that your payment
      provider cannot send an automated reminder &mdash; this is the most likely way you cause real
      pain, and it is entirely preventable.
    </li>
    <li>Who on your team is told, and how they are supported.</li>
  </ul>
  <p style="margin-top: 2mm">
    Rehearse it once, out loud, before you need it. It is a grim hour and it is the single
    highest-value hour of preparation available to this company. <span class="ev i">INFERENCE</span>
  </p>
</div>

<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-19">19&nbsp;&nbsp;When I would tell you to stop</h2>

<p class="lede">
  A chief of staff who cannot say this is not doing the job. These are the conditions under which
  continuing would be the wrong call, written now while neither of us is invested in the answer.
</p>

<h3>Stop, or change something fundamental</h3>
<div class="kv">
  <div>
    <span
      >Fewer than half of paying families reach a first approved memory, after two attempts to fix
      it</span
    ><span>the split incentive is fatal as designed</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Cost to serve exceeds price and no automation path is visible by 100 archives</span
    ><span>the arithmetic does not close</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Two channels tested properly, neither produced families repeatably</span
    ><span>there is no distribution, and nothing else matters</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span
      >Counsel's answer on third parties in memories requires a change that breaks the product</span
    ><span>rethink the shape, not the effort</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>You cannot raise and cannot fund the launch gate</span
    ><span>do not launch under-secured &mdash; stop instead</span>
  </div>
</div>

<h3>Reasons that are not reasons to stop</h3>
<div class="kv">
  <div>
    <span>It is growing more slowly than you hoped</span
    ><span>expected; the verdict is delayed by design</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>A competitor with voice cloning raises a large round</span
    ><span>that is your positioning arriving, not your market leaving</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Engagement metrics look bad</span><span>you should not be measuring them (§12)</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>Someone tells you the market is too small</span><span>answer with §2, then carry on</span>
  </div>
  <div>
    <span>It is emotionally heavy work</span
    ><span>true, and a reason to staff and supervise it properly &mdash; not to stop</span>
  </div>
</div>

<div class="callout ok">
  <span class="label">And the one that outranks all of them</span>
  <p>
    If continuing would require removing the refusal &mdash; the voice, the face, the persona, the
    simulation of someone who died &mdash; then the honest answer is that the company you would be
    continuing is not this one. Stop, or sell it to someone bound by §17, and be at peace with
    either. A version of EverEcho that simulates people is not a compromised EverEcho; it is the
    thing EverEcho was built to be an alternative to.
  </p>
</div>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/60-part6-a.html`

```html
<div class="part-divider">
  <div class="kicker">Part VI</div>
  <h2>Your operating system</h2>
  <p>
    The cadence that keeps this on track, the first thirty days in detail, and every decision
    currently waiting on you.
  </p>
</div>

<h2 id="sec-20">20&nbsp;&nbsp;The cadence</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Founders do not fail from lack of effort; they fail from losing the thread. A fixed cadence is how
  you notice a problem in week three instead of month five.
</p>

<h3>Every Monday &mdash; 45 minutes, alone</h3>
<ol class="runbook">
  <li>
    <strong>Read the audit trail.</strong> Not a summary &mdash; the actual log, including refusals.
    Your own readiness document names this as a condition for piloting, and it is also how you find
    risk&nbsp;7 before someone else does. Fifteen minutes.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>The five metrics from §12.</strong> Written down, in the same place, every week, so the
    trend is visible rather than remembered.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>The abstention band.</strong> Movement in either direction is an incident until proven
    otherwise.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Open decisions (§22).</strong> Anything sitting for more than two weeks is either not
    important or being avoided. Decide which, out loud.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>One sentence:</strong> what is the single most important thing this week? Write it where
    you will see it on Thursday.
  </li>
</ol>

<h3>Every month &mdash; 2 hours</h3>
<ul>
  <li>
    <strong>Cohort margin.</strong> The §2 margin trap alarm. If it is not improving, say so plainly
    in writing rather than assuming next month.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Unit costs against reality.</strong> Provider invoices attributed to archives. Hours
    logged and costed, including yours.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>The falsification thresholds from §8.</strong> Reread them. They were written by a more
    objective version of you.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>One customer conversation you did not need to have.</strong> Not a support ticket
    &mdash; a conversation.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Update the decision log.</strong> The company deserves the same discipline the codebase
    got.
  </li>
</ul>

<h3>Every quarter &mdash; half a day</h3>
<ul>
  <li><strong>Are you at the stage you thought?</strong> Against §16, honestly.</li>
  <li>
    <strong>Risk register review (§18).</strong> Likelihoods change. So do the early-warning signs.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>The refusal audit.</strong> Has anything shipped that weakens it? Do the enforcing tests
    still exist and still run? Has anyone asked you to remove it, and what did you say?
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Governance progress (§17).</strong> Which instruments are in place, which are still
    intentions.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Your own state.</strong> Risk&nbsp;5 is you. It is a real line item and it does not
    appear on any dashboard.
  </li>
</ul>

<div class="callout">
  <span class="label">Keep a decision log for the company</span>
  <p>
    The repository has one &mdash; fifteen decisions, each with its reasoning, which is why the
    architecture is still coherent. Do the same for the business: the decision, the date, the
    reasoning, what would change your mind. In eighteen months you will not remember why you chose a
    price, a channel or a jurisdiction, and the reasoning is worth more than the choice.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-21">21&nbsp;&nbsp;The first thirty days</h2>

<div class="horizon">
  <span class="h-n">Day 1 &ndash; Day 30</span>
  <span>Concrete. In order. Start the external clocks first.</span>
  <span class="h-when">Starting Monday</span>
</div>

<p class="eyebrow">Days 1&ndash;2 &mdash; things that cost hours and buy weeks</p>
<ul class="check">
  <li>Fix the pricing-page tense so the site claims no families you do not have</li>
  <li>Name yourself as the accountable person in <code>INCIDENT_RUNBOOK.md</code>, commit it</li>
  <li>Begin trademark clearance on the name</li>
  <li>
    Send the §5 brief to two or three data-protection lawyers; ask each the deceased-persons
    question
  </li>
  <li>Email three candidate security reviewers for availability and cost in week 6</li>
  <li>Ask two disability organisations about a paid accessibility review in week 7</li>
</ul>

<p class="eyebrow">Days 3&ndash;7 &mdash; decide what is yours to decide</p>
<ul class="check">
  <li>
    Work through §5 decisions 2, 5, 6 and 7; write each into the company decision log with its
    reasoning
  </li>
  <li>Draft the prohibitions as customer-facing terms (§17, instrument 1)</li>
  <li>Choose the hosting provider and region</li>
  <li>List every development secret that must be replaced</li>
</ul>

<p class="eyebrow">Days 8&ndash;14 &mdash; the biggest engineering piece</p>
<ul class="check">
  <li>
    Production authentication: OIDC or passkeys, MFA enrolment, <strong>and password reset</strong>
  </li>
  <li>Real secrets in a secret manager; no <code>dev-only-…</code> string survives</li>
  <li>Deploy to a real environment for the first time, with synthetic data only</li>
</ul>

<p class="eyebrow">Days 15&ndash;21 &mdash; make the unproven things proven</p>
<ul class="check">
  <li>Run all eight integrations, in the §6 order, checking the stated first thing for each</li>
  <li>
    <strong>Record your real unit costs as you go</strong> &mdash; this is the week the §2 worksheet
    gets filled in
  </li>
  <li>Wire Stripe webhook signature verification; test a payment and a refund end to end</li>
  <li>
    Compare the local extractive composer against the hosted one, and decide whether you need the
    hosted one at all
  </li>
</ul>

<p class="eyebrow">Days 22&ndash;30 &mdash; the things that are skipped</p>
<ul class="check">
  <li>Encryption at rest with a customer-managed key</li>
  <li>A real malware scanner in the upload path</li>
  <li>Backups configured, and a restore <em>performed</em> into a clean environment and timed</li>
  <li>A deletion performed end to end and verified against the database, not the receipt</li>
  <li>Monitoring and alerting that reach your phone</li>
  <li>Inspect logs, error reports and the support view for memory content; fix anything found</li>
  <li><strong>Write the death runbook (§18) and read it aloud once</strong></li>
  <li>Set the provisional price and update the pricing page</li>
</ul>

<div class="callout ok">
  <span class="label">At the end of day 30 you should have</span>
  <p>
    A deployed system with real authentication, proven integrations, known unit costs, a price,
    working billing, and every external clock running. What you will <em>not</em> have is a single
    real memory in the database &mdash; and that is correct. Weeks 5&ndash;8 close the launch gate;
    the first family comes after it, not before.
  </p>
</div>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/parts/61-part6-b.html`

```html
<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-22">22&nbsp;&nbsp;Open decisions, waiting on you</h2>

<p class="lede">
  Everything in this document that requires a human judgement, consolidated. Nothing here can be
  delegated, deferred indefinitely, or resolved by more engineering.
</p>

<table>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th style="width: 5%">#</th>
      <th style="width: 28%">Decision</th>
      <th style="width: 13%">By when</th>
      <th style="width: 11%">Where</th>
      <th>My recommendation</th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <td>1</td>
      <td>Keep the name or rename</td>
      <td>Week 3</td>
      <td>§5</td>
      <td>Clear it now; rename immediately if not clearly clearable</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>2</td>
      <td>Jurisdiction and data region</td>
      <td>Week 2</td>
      <td>§5</td>
      <td>Where your first ten families are, not your hundred-thousandth</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>3</td>
      <td>Which counsel, and engage them</td>
      <td>Week 1</td>
      <td>§5</td>
      <td>Data-protection specialist; test them on deceased-persons data</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>4</td>
      <td>Named accountable person</td>
      <td>Day 1</td>
      <td>§5</td>
      <td>You, in writing, today</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>5</td>
      <td>Audio-first, or audio and video</td>
      <td>Week 2</td>
      <td>§5</td>
      <td>Audio default; video as a priced upgrade with a stated term</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>6</td>
      <td>The provisional price</td>
      <td>Week 4</td>
      <td>§5, §9</td>
      <td>Capture fee large, preservation annual, family access free</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>7</td>
      <td>What lapse in payment means</td>
      <td>Before first sale</td>
      <td>§9</td>
      <td>Long grace, then export-and-close on a stated schedule</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>8</td>
      <td>Prepaid preservation: offer it or not</td>
      <td>Before first sale</td>
      <td>§9</td>
      <td>Only after counsel answers brief item 11, and never as &ldquo;forever&rdquo;</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>9</td>
      <td>Which channel to test first</td>
      <td>Week 6</td>
      <td>§10</td>
      <td>Estate and private-client advisers; one partner only</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>10</td>
      <td>The falsification thresholds</td>
      <td>Before family 1</td>
      <td>§8</td>
      <td>Write them down and date them while you are still objective</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>11</td>
      <td>Bootstrap or raise</td>
      <td>Month 5</td>
      <td>§14</td>
      <td>Bootstrap through the first ten; then raise small, from aligned investors</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>12</td>
      <td>Which governance instruments, and when</td>
      <td>Weeks 2&ndash;4</td>
      <td>§17</td>
      <td>Instruments 1, 2 and 6 now; 3 and 5 into the first round; 4 at stage 1</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>13</td>
      <td>Whether to publish the readiness document</td>
      <td>Month 1</td>
      <td>§4</td>
      <td>Yes. It is the cheapest credibility available to you</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>14</td>
      <td>Hosted composition, or keep the extractive one</td>
      <td>Week 3</td>
      <td>§6</td>
      <td>Test both on real people before you assume you need the fluent one</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <td>15</td>
      <td>What unapproved material means after a death</td>
      <td>Before family 1</td>
      <td>§18</td>
      <td>The hardest question here, and it has no default. Decide it while it is abstract</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>

<div class="callout warn">
  <span class="label">Three of these are quietly urgent</span>
  <p>
    <strong>#4</strong> takes ten minutes and is currently blocking your own launch gate.
    <strong>#3</strong> runs on someone else's calendar and gates everything legal.
    <strong>#15</strong> is the one you will be tempted to leave until it happens &mdash; and it is
    the one you will handle worst if you do.
  </p>
</div>

<div class="page-break"></div>
<h2 id="sec-23">A closing note</h2>

<p class="lede">
  You asked me to guide you to a unicorn. I have given you the arithmetic that outcome requires, the
  sequence that makes it possible, and the places where I think it most likely breaks. Here is what
  I actually believe.
</p>

<p>
  The hardest thing about this company is not the technology, and you have already proved that by
  finishing the part everyone else fakes. It is that you have chosen a business whose central
  promise is a refusal &mdash; and refusals do not demo, do not go viral, and do not respond to the
  ordinary levers. Every structural problem in §3 traces back to that single choice.
</p>

<p>
  It is still the right choice, and not for sentimental reasons. It is the only version of this
  product that institutions can adopt, that reluctant storytellers will fill honestly, and that
  survives the moment when the first simulation company is publicly disgraced. You are not building
  a safer version of a category. You are building the version that is left standing.
</p>

<p>What I would hold you to, if I were actually sitting beside you:</p>
<ul>
  <li>
    <strong>Do not choose a cheap price.</strong> It is the one decision that forecloses everything
    you asked me about, and it is usually made in an afternoon by someone who feels awkward asking
    for money.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Do not put a real memory in that database before the gate in §7 closes.</strong> Not
    one. Not your own grandmother's.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Bind the refusal while it is easy</strong> &mdash; before investors, before an acquirer,
    before a bad quarter makes it feel negotiable.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Keep doing the interviews yourself</strong> long past the point it feels like a good use
    of your time. It is where the product actually comes from.
  </li>
  <li>
    <strong>Publish what is not finished.</strong> The readiness document, the gaps, the things that
    never ran. It is your strangest asset and your most durable one.
  </li>
</ul>

<p>
  And one honest thing about the word in your question. Nobody can hand you a unicorn, and this
  document has not tried to. What it has tried to do is make sure that if this company does not
  become one, it will be for reasons outside your control &mdash; not because you priced it cheaply
  in month two, launched before it was safe, or traded away the promise in a difficult week.
</p>

<p>
  A thousand families with an intact promise is a real company and a good life's work. Fifty
  thousand is the arithmetic in §2. Both begin the same way: fix a sentence on your pricing page,
  name yourself accountable, send the brief to counsel, and start the clock.
</p>

<p style="margin-top: 8mm" class="footnote">
  Every claim in this document is labelled with its evidence class. Nothing here is a market figure
  I could not verify, a statistic I could not source, or a projection presented as a fact. It was
  written to the same standard as the product it describes, which seemed like the only defensible
  way to write it.
</p>
```

## `docs/briefing/src/render.mjs`

```javascript
import { chromium } from '@playwright/test';
import path from 'node:path';
import { fileURLToPath } from 'node:url';

const here = path.dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));
const input = process.env.EVERECHO_DOC_HTML ?? path.join(here, 'document.html');
const output =
  process.env.EVERECHO_DOC_PDF ??
  path.join(here, '..', '..', 'EverEcho-Chief-of-Staff-Briefing.pdf');

const browser = await chromium.launch({
  executablePath: process.env.PLAYWRIGHT_CHROMIUM_PATH || undefined,
});
const page = await browser.newPage();
await page.goto(`file://${input}`, { waitUntil: 'load' });
await page.emulateMedia({ media: 'print' });

const footer = `
<div style="width:100%;font-family:system-ui,sans-serif;font-size:7pt;color:#8a857c;
            padding:0 16mm;display:flex;justify-content:space-between;align-items:center;">
  <span>EverEcho &mdash; Chief of Staff Briefing</span>
  <span class="pageNumber"></span>
</div>`;

await page.pdf({
  path: output,
  format: 'A4',
  printBackground: true,
  tagged: true,
  outline: true,
  displayHeaderFooter: true,
  headerTemplate: '<div></div>',
  footerTemplate: footer,
  margin: { top: '18mm', bottom: '20mm', left: '16mm', right: '16mm' },
});

await browser.close();
console.log(`rendered ${output}`);
```

## `docs/pitch/README.md`

````markdown
# The pitch-and-manual document

`docs/EverEcho-v0.1-Pitch-and-Manual.pdf` — 57 pages, A4, with a linked table of
contents and PDF bookmarks. It is the whole project in one document: the pitch,
the manual, and the technical record including the honest production-readiness
verdict.

## What is in it

| Part | Sections | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| I — The pitch | 1–8 | The problem, what EverEcho is and is not, why the boundary is the product, the six roles, the consent architecture, provenance, and the measured evidence |
| II — The manual | 9–13 | Getting it running, the demonstration archive, all 16 screens with commentary, the command reference, and troubleshooting |
| III — Under the hood | 14–20 | Architecture, the data model, security and privacy engineering, what was measured, the readiness verdict, the next five actions, and a repository map |

Every figure is a screenshot of the application running locally against a real
PostgreSQL 16 database. There are no mockups in it, and no figure was projected
or estimated.

## Rebuilding it

The document is print-styled HTML rendered to PDF by headless Chromium.

```bash
# 1. Capture the screenshots (needs the stack running and seeded)
#    into a directory of PNGs named 01-landing.png … 16-tablet-overview.png
# 2. Point SHOTS in src/assemble.py at that directory, then:
python3 src/assemble.py          # inlines the PNGs as data URIs -> document.html
node src/render.mjs              # document.html -> the PDF
```

`src/parts/*.html` are concatenated in filename order, so section order is the
filename order. `src/style.css` holds the A4 print stylesheet: `@page` rules,
the cover, part dividers, callouts, tables, figures and badges.

The screenshots themselves are not committed — they are regenerated by running
the application, which is the only way this document stays honest about showing
software that actually runs.
````

## `docs/pitch/src/assemble.py`

```python
import base64, glob, os, re, sys

BUILD = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
SHOTS = os.environ.get('EVERECHO_SHOTS', './screenshots')

css = open(os.path.join(BUILD, 'style.css')).read()

body = []
for p in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(BUILD, 'parts', '*.html'))):
    body.append(open(p).read())
body = '\n'.join(body)

# Replace {{IMG:name}} with base64 data URIs
missing = []
def sub(m):
    name = m.group(1)
    path = os.path.join(SHOTS, name)
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        missing.append(name)
        return f'<!-- MISSING {name} -->'
    data = base64.b64encode(open(path, 'rb').read()).decode()
    return f'<img src="data:image/png;base64,{data}" alt="{name}">'

body, n = re.subn(r'\{\{IMG:([^}]+)\}\}', sub, body)
if missing:
    print('MISSING IMAGES:', missing); sys.exit(1)

html = f"""<title>EverEcho v0.1 — Pitch and Manual</title>
<style>
{css}
</style>
{body}
"""

out = os.path.join(BUILD, 'document.html')
open(out, 'w').write(html)
print(f'embedded {n} images; wrote {out} ({len(html)/1024/1024:.1f} MB)')
```
